screens.title: Create and Assign a Material
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through creating a material and assigning it so you can see live results. First, create a new Material asset by right-clicking in the Project window, choose Create, and then Material. Give it a descriptive name like M_SciFiPanel or M_WoodFloor so you can find it later. Second, select the target 3D object in the Hierarchy, for example a Plane or a Cube. Third, drag the new material from the Project window onto the object in the Scene view or onto the object name in the Hierarchy. The mesh updates immediately to show the material's current settings. Fourth, open the material in the Inspector to access the Standard Shader parameters. Use Albedo to set a base color or assign an Albedo texture, then adjust Metallic and Smoothness to begin shaping the surface response. A common misconception is that the material must be assigned before you edit it. In fact, you can edit the material asset first and then assign it, or assign and edit while observing the object. The key is to keep your material assets organized and preview changes in the Scene to validate scale and lighting. Practice this flow until creating and applying materials becomes second nature.

content.html:
Process Flow

Create & Assign

Follow these numbered steps to create a new Material asset and apply it to geometry so you can edit and preview it live.

  1. Create Material. Right-click in Project → Create → Material. Name it descriptively for reuse.
  2. Select Target. Pick a Plane, Cube, or model in the Hierarchy to test the material.
  3. Assign Material. Drag the material onto the object or its name in the Hierarchy.
  4. Open Inspector. Edit Albedo, Metallic, Smoothness and add textures as needed.
Key Takeaway

Assign materials to test meshes and iterate in the Scene. Naming and organization speed up reuse.

Visual Steps
1. Create Material asset (M_SciFiPanel)
2. Select Plane or model to preview
3. Drag material onto object → immediate update
4. Open Inspector to edit shader properties
Example:
Create M_SciFiPanel, assign it to a Plane, then tweak Albedo and Smoothness to preview a reflective panel.

screens.title: Standard Shader: Albedo, Metallic, Smoothness
screens.narratorSegment: The Standard Shader exposes core properties that define surface response. Albedo is the material's base color; it can be a flat color or a detailed texture. Think of Albedo as the information that determines diffuse reflection and visible color under neutral lighting. Metallic is a value from zero to one that dictates whether the material behaves like a metal. Metals reflect their environment with tinted highlights and generally do not show diffuse color in the same way non-metals do. Smoothness controls how sharp or blurred highlights appear; high smoothness yields sharp, mirror-like reflections, while low smoothness scatters specular response and looks rough. A common misconception is to set Metallic and Smoothness independently without considering physical plausibility. For example, wood should have Metallic near zero, but it might vary Smoothness for varnished versus raw wood. When you increase Metallic, the material will rely more on environment reflections; increasing Smoothness tightens the reflection. Experiment with values: try Albedo dark gray, Metallic high, Smoothness high to make a polished metal; or Albedo brown, Metallic zero, Smoothness low to make a rough wood. That contrast helps you internalize how sliders produce material types.

keyIdea.title: PBR Essentials
keyIdea.text: Albedo sets base color, Metallic toggles metal behavior, and Smoothness controls highlight sharpness. Together they create physically plausible surfaces.

content.html:
Definition

Albedo · Metallic · Smoothness

Albedo: Base color or texture that defines diffuse appearance.

Metallic: 0–1 slider; metals reflect environment and tint specular highlights.

Smoothness: Controls highlight sharpness; high values yield mirror-like reflections.

Key Takeaway

Treat these three as a set: adjust them together to produce convincing materials like metal, plastic, or wood.

Examples & Contrast
Polished Metal: Albedo dark grey, Metallic 1.0, Smoothness 0.9
Varnished Wood: Albedo brown texture, Metallic 0.0, Smoothness 0.6
Rubber: Albedo colored, Metallic 0.0, Smoothness 0.2
Misconception
Don't make non-metals metallic to fake brightness. Metals and non-metals reflect light differently; mixing that expectation breaks realism.

screens.title: Texture Maps: Albedo, Normal, Metallic, Smoothness, Occlusion
screens.narratorSegment: Texture maps give materials their detailed surface information. Albedo provides color detail — use it instead of a flat color when you want realistic patterns like wood grain or bricks. Normal maps encode surface microdetail as directional data; they are encoded into RGB channels and must be imported as Normal Map so Unity interprets the blue-purple information correctly. Metallic maps often use grayscale or packed channels to indicate metalness per pixel; when using a metallic texture, ensure the shader expects the correct channel (Metallic and Smoothness maps sometimes share or pack data). Smoothness can be baked into a texture or controlled by a slider; a smoothness map modulates specular sharpness across the surface. Occlusion maps darken crevices to simulate ambient shadowing. A common mistake is placing a normal map into the Albedo slot — this produces wrong colors because normals are not surface color. Always check import type and sRGB flags: color maps generally use sRGB, while Normal maps and masks use linear color space. Example: assign wood_albedo. png to Albedo, wood_normal. png to Normal Map, wood_metallic. png to Metallic, and wood_smoothness. png to Smoothness, then verify each map's import type and visual effect.

keyIdea.title: Map Roles
keyIdea.text: Assign each texture to the appropriate slot and confirm import settings: Albedo for color, Normal for surface normals, Metallic and Smoothness for reflectivity, Occlusion for crevice shading.

content.html:
Definition

Texture Map Roles

  • Albedo: Color detail and patterning; usually sRGB.
  • Normal Map: Encodes surface direction, import as Normal Map to read correctly.
  • Metallic: Grayscale or packed channel defining metalness per pixel.
  • Smoothness: Controls specular blur; may be a slider or a texture channel.
  • Occlusion: Ambient occlusion mask to darken crevices.
Practical Example
Assign wood_albedo.png to Albedo and ensure it is sRGB for correct color.
Import wood_normal.png as Normal Map to add bump detail without changing geometry.
Use wood_metallic.png only if parts of the material are metallic; otherwise set Metallic to 0.
Check each map in the Inspector and preview with lighting to confirm correct visual results.

screens.title: Tiling & Offset: Control Texture Placement
screens.narratorSegment: Tiling and Offset are simple but powerful controls for how a texture maps onto a surface. Tiling multiplies a texture across U and V directions. For example, setting Tiling X and Y to two repeats the texture twice horizontally and vertically, making the pattern elements appear smaller on the model. Use this when a texture looks too large for the model, like bricks that span an entire wall. Offset shifts the texture coordinate origin, letting you slide a pattern along a surface without altering the UVs. If Offset X is set to 0.5, the texture starts halfway across its width, effectively shifting the pattern. In practical workflow, change Tiling to match apparent scale, then nudge Offset to hide seams or align features. Beware of over-tiling: very high tiling values create obvious repetition and can reveal seams. A good approach is to combine reasonable tiling values with varied textures or detail maps to break repetition. Example: set Tiling to 5,5 for a small sci-fi panel pattern on a plane, then use Offset to place a central emblem. This produces a dense, detailed surface without stretching.

keyIdea.title: Placement Controls
keyIdea.text: Use Tiling to repeat textures and Offset to shift them; balance tiling values to avoid visible repetition and maintain natural scale.

content.html:
Process

Tiling & Offset Steps

  1. Open the Material Inspector and locate Tiling & Offset.
  2. Increase Tiling X/Y to repeat the texture more times across the surface.
  3. Use Offset X/Y to move the texture origin and align patterns or hide seams.
  4. Preview in Scene and reduce tiling if repetition becomes obvious.
Tip: Combine moderate tiling with varied detail maps or decals to break up repetition.
Concrete Example
Plane with sci-fi grid texture: set Tiling to 5,5 to make grid smaller and more detailed.
If emblem sits off-center, adjust Offset X to 0.2 until it aligns with model features.
Common Mistake

Avoid extremely high tiling values that create obvious repetition artifacts. Instead, tile moderately and add variation with decals or AO maps.

screens.title: Color Tinting and Emission
screens.narratorSegment: Color tinting and emission are flexible tools for creating variations without authoring new textures. Albedo tint multiplies the color information of an Albedo texture so you can shift a stone from gray to a mossy green or warm it toward orange for a volcanic feel. This is particularly useful when you need multiple color variants of the same texture without duplicating texture files. Emission makes parts of the material appear to glow. Enable the Emission checkbox, choose an Emission Color, and optionally assign an Emission Map. The map determines which areas glow and with what intensity. Increasing the Emission Intensity makes the glow more pronounced on the object's surface. A common misconception is that emission automatically lights nearby objects. By default, emission only makes the object appear to emit light. To actually illuminate the environment in real time, add point or spot lights or use baked Global Illumination so emission contributes to lightmaps. In practice, use emission for screens, indicators, and decorative glows, and combine it with small point lights when interactive illumination is required. Color Tinting and Emission means tint the albedo to create color variants and use emission with maps to add controllable glow; add lights or baked gi for real illumination.. In practical terms, use albedo tint and emission to vary appearance and add glow. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition

Color Tinting & Emission

Albedo Tint: Multiplies the texture color so you can produce variations without new textures.

Emission: Adds self-lit color to the material; use an Emission Map to localize glow.

Intensity: Scales how bright the emission appears on the surface.

Misconception: Emission does not automatically cast real-time light onto other objects unless you add lights or bake GI.
Concrete Example
Use the same Albedo texture and tint it green to create a mossy variation quickly.
Enable Emission, assign the pattern as Emission Map, set color to cyan and Intensity to 2 for a glowing panel effect.
Pro Tip

Use emission selectively for readable indicators and pair with small lights for believable interactive illumination.

screens.title: Hands-on Activity: Glowing Sci‑Fi Panel
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on procedure turns our concepts into a small lab you can follow. Start with an empty scene and create a Plane via Hierarchy → 3D Object → Plane. Next, in the Project window, right-click and Create → Material and name it M_SciFiPanel. Assign the material to the Plane by dragging it onto the object. Import a simple patterned texture as your Albedo; if it's black and white it can also serve as an Emission map. Convert or import a Normal map for depth; set its Texture Type to Normal Map in import settings. In the material Inspector, assign the Albedo texture, assign the Normal Map, and set Tiling to 5,5 to make the pattern dense on the plane. Increase Metallic to 0.8 and Smoothness to 0.7 for a polished feel. Enable Emission, drop the same patterned texture into the Emission slot, choose a vibrant color like blue or green, and raise Intensity to 2 or 3 to make the pattern glow. Finally, experiment with Offset to position motifs and, if you need the emission to light the scene, add a Point Light near the panel or bake Global Illumination. This sequence gives a repeatable workflow for a polished emissive surface.

keyIdea.title: Lab Sequence
keyIdea.text: Create Plane → new Material → assign textures and normal map → adjust Tiling → set Metallic/Smoothness → enable Emission → refine Offset and lighting.

content.html:
Lab Walkthrough

Build a Glowing Panel

1. Create Plane: Hierarchy → 3D Object → Plane
2. Create Material: Project → Create → Material → M_SciFiPanel
3. Assign textures: Albedo (pattern), Normal Map, optional Metallic/Smoothness maps
4. Tiling: set X,Y to 5 to shrink pattern; Offset as needed to align motifs
5. Set Metallic 0.8, Smoothness 0.7 for a polished look
6. Enable Emission: assign map, pick color, increase Intensity to 2–3
7. If you need real light: add small Point Light or bake GI for emissive contribution
Example Values
Tiling: 5,5
Metallic: 0.8
Smoothness: 0.7
Emission Intensity: 2–3
Safety Tip
Avoid excessive tiling which reveals repetition. Use decals or variation maps to break patterns.

screens.title: Common Mistakes & Troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: Troubleshooting starts by checking the obvious places. If your object displays strange purple-blue colors, you likely placed a Normal map into the Albedo slot or forgot to mark it as a Normal Map in import settings. Inspect each texture slot to ensure the correct image is assigned. Next, review import settings: color maps should use sRGB, while Normal and mask textures should use linear. Another frequent issue is unrealistic slider combinations: giving a wooden object a high Metallic value produces unnatural reflections. If emission appears bright on the object but doesn't light the scene, remember emission only makes the surface glow; it doesn't create real-time illumination unless you add lights or bake Global Illumination. When tiling looks wrong, check the model's UV scale; high tiling values may also highlight repetition and seams, so combine tiling with variation layers. Finally, use a neutral test mesh and consistent lighting to compare materials; changes are easier to judge on a flat plane under a controlled environment. These checks will catch most problems quickly and get you back to iteration. Comparison

Problem vs Expectation

Problem: Purple or wrong colors on material.
Fix: Ensure Normal map is imported as Normal Map and placed in the Normal slot.
Problem: Bright emission, no scene illumination.
Fix: Add real lights for dynamic illumination or enable baked Global Illumination for emission contribution.
Problem: Textures look oversized or stretched.
Fix: Adjust Tiling and check model UVs; reduce tiling to hide repetition and fix seams with offset or decals.
Checklist
  • Confirm each texture is in the correct slot.
  • Verify import type: Normal Map vs sRGB color textures.
  • Use physically plausible Metallic/Smoothness combinations.
  • Test on a neutral plane under consistent lighting.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Maps & Lighting
screens.narratorSegment: These final concepts focus on texture maps and lighting behavior. Tiling determines how many times a texture repeats across a model's U and V axes, and Offset shifts the texture's starting point across the surface. Both are essential for matching texture scale to model geometry and hiding seams. Emission and Emission Maps make a surface appear to glow; however, emission does not automatically cast real-time light onto other objects. To make emissive surfaces illuminate their environment, add a light component such as a Point Light, or enable emission contribution to baked Global Illumination and perform a lightmap bake. Lastly, always validate import settings: Normal maps must be set to Normal Map import type to display correctly, and color textures typically use sRGB. These practices prevent common errors and keep your materials integrated with scene lighting.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we put material theory into practice by creating and refining materials inside Unity. You will learn the exact steps to create a new Material asset, assign it to a model, and shape its visual qualities using the Standard Shader properties. We will show how Albedo color, Metallic and Smoothness sliders interact to produce plastic, metal, or rough surfaces. Then we move beyond color to add texture maps — Albedo for color detail, Normal maps for surface relief, Metallic and Smoothness maps for physical response, and Occlusion for shadowing. You will also learn how Tiling and Offset let you scale and shift textures to match model scale, and how Albedo tinting plus Emission opens quick variations and glowing details. Finally, we'll preview a hands-on lab that walks you through creating a glowing sci-fi panel on a plane, adjusting tiling, and enabling emission correctly. Notice common mistakes along the way, like putting a normal map into the Albedo slot or expecting emission to cast real-time light without adding a light source or baking GI. By the end you'll have clear, repeatable workflows for creating materials and controlling texture placement to produce consistent, realistic surfaces.

These objectives map to the practical skills you'll practice in the lab. First, you'll create a new Material asset and assign it to scene geometry so you can see visual changes live. This is a fundamental workflow: assets live in the Project window, and dragging a material onto an object updates that object's surface immediately. Second, you'll adjust the Standard Shader's primary controls: Albedo color for base tinting, Metallic for metalness, and Smoothness for specular spread. Understanding how these three interact is vital for telling metal from non-metal materials. Third, you'll apply texture maps—Albedo, Normal, Metallic, Smoothness, and Occlusion—to add detail and realism. Correct slot assignment and import settings are crucial to avoid color or normal map display errors. Fourth, you'll control how textures repeat and shift using Tiling and Offset, which helps match texture scale to model size. Each objective focuses on an applied skill and why it matters: assignment for workflow speed, shader sliders for accurate PBR, maps for surface detail, and tiling for correct scale. Practice these deliberately and verify results in the Scene view and Inspector.

This second objectives screen focuses on translating those skills into reliable habits. Start by naming your materials clearly — for example M_WoodFloor or M_SciFiMetal — so you can reuse and tweak them quickly. When you assign a material and tweak the Inspector, observe immediate visual feedback in the Scene; this lets you iterate until the look matches scale and lighting. Learn to judge metallic and smoothness values physically: metals should have high metallic and high smoothness for sharp highlights, whereas wood or stone have near-zero metallic values and lower smoothness. Practice importing textures with correct types — Normal maps must be marked as Normal Map so Unity interprets their blue-purple encoding correctly. Use Tiling to increase repetition when a texture looks oversized, and Offset to nudge seams or align motifs. Finally, treat Emission as a surface glow, not a real light source unless you bake GI or add actual lights. These habits keep your materials predictable and integrate them cleanly into a scene's lighting environment.

Let's walk through creating a material and assigning it so you can see live results. First, create a new Material asset by right-clicking in the Project window, choose Create, and then Material. Give it a descriptive name like M_SciFiPanel or M_WoodFloor so you can find it later. Second, select the target 3D object in the Hierarchy, for example a Plane or a Cube. Third, drag the new material from the Project window onto the object in the Scene view or onto the object name in the Hierarchy. The mesh updates immediately to show the material's current settings. Fourth, open the material in the Inspector to access the Standard Shader parameters. Use Albedo to set a base color or assign an Albedo texture, then adjust Metallic and Smoothness to begin shaping the surface response. A common misconception is that the material must be assigned before you edit it. In fact, you can edit the material asset first and then assign it, or assign and edit while observing the object. The key is to keep your material assets organized and preview changes in the Scene to validate scale and lighting. Practice this flow until creating and applying materials becomes second nature.

The Standard Shader exposes core properties that define surface response. Albedo is the material's base color; it can be a flat color or a detailed texture. Think of Albedo as the information that determines diffuse reflection and visible color under neutral lighting. Metallic is a value from zero to one that dictates whether the material behaves like a metal. Metals reflect their environment with tinted highlights and generally do not show diffuse color in the same way non-metals do. Smoothness controls how sharp or blurred highlights appear; high smoothness yields sharp, mirror-like reflections, while low smoothness scatters specular response and looks rough. A common misconception is to set Metallic and Smoothness independently without considering physical plausibility. For example, wood should have Metallic near zero, but it might vary Smoothness for varnished versus raw wood. When you increase Metallic, the material will rely more on environment reflections; increasing Smoothness tightens the reflection. Experiment with values: try Albedo dark gray, Metallic high, Smoothness high to make a polished metal; or Albedo brown, Metallic zero, Smoothness low to make a rough wood. That contrast helps you internalize how sliders produce material types.

Texture maps give materials their detailed surface information. Albedo provides color detail — use it instead of a flat color when you want realistic patterns like wood grain or bricks. Normal maps encode surface microdetail as directional data; they are encoded into RGB channels and must be imported as Normal Map so Unity interprets the blue-purple information correctly. Metallic maps often use grayscale or packed channels to indicate metalness per pixel; when using a metallic texture, ensure the shader expects the correct channel (Metallic and Smoothness maps sometimes share or pack data). Smoothness can be baked into a texture or controlled by a slider; a smoothness map modulates specular sharpness across the surface. Occlusion maps darken crevices to simulate ambient shadowing. A common mistake is placing a normal map into the Albedo slot — this produces wrong colors because normals are not surface color. Always check import type and sRGB flags: color maps generally use sRGB, while Normal maps and masks use linear color space. Example: assign wood_albedo. png to Albedo, wood_normal. png to Normal Map, wood_metallic. png to Metallic, and wood_smoothness. png to Smoothness, then verify each map's import type and visual effect.

Tiling and Offset are simple but powerful controls for how a texture maps onto a surface. Tiling multiplies a texture across U and V directions. For example, setting Tiling X and Y to two repeats the texture twice horizontally and vertically, making the pattern elements appear smaller on the model. Use this when a texture looks too large for the model, like bricks that span an entire wall. Offset shifts the texture coordinate origin, letting you slide a pattern along a surface without altering the UVs. If Offset X is set to 0.5, the texture starts halfway across its width, effectively shifting the pattern. In practical workflow, change Tiling to match apparent scale, then nudge Offset to hide seams or align features. Beware of over-tiling: very high tiling values create obvious repetition and can reveal seams. A good approach is to combine reasonable tiling values with varied textures or detail maps to break repetition. Example: set Tiling to 5,5 for a small sci-fi panel pattern on a plane, then use Offset to place a central emblem. This produces a dense, detailed surface without stretching.

Color tinting and emission are flexible tools for creating variations without authoring new textures. Albedo tint multiplies the color information of an Albedo texture so you can shift a stone from gray to a mossy green or warm it toward orange for a volcanic feel. This is particularly useful when you need multiple color variants of the same texture without duplicating texture files. Emission makes parts of the material appear to glow. Enable the Emission checkbox, choose an Emission Color, and optionally assign an Emission Map. The map determines which areas glow and with what intensity. Increasing the Emission Intensity makes the glow more pronounced on the object's surface. A common misconception is that emission automatically lights nearby objects. By default, emission only makes the object appear to emit light. To actually illuminate the environment in real time, add point or spot lights or use baked Global Illumination so emission contributes to lightmaps. In practice, use emission for screens, indicators, and decorative glows, and combine it with small point lights when interactive illumination is required. Color Tinting and Emission means tint the albedo to create color variants and use emission with maps to add controllable glow; add lights or baked gi for real illumination.. In practical terms, use albedo tint and emission to vary appearance and add glow. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.
